claim: In Heliconius butterflies, wing colour pattern diversity and scale types are controlled by a few genes of large effect.
source: In Heliconius butterflies, wing colour pattern diversity and scale types are controlled by a few genes of large effect that regulate colour pattern switches between morphs and species across a large mimetic radiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general claim about Heliconius butterflies.

claim: cortex has been repeatedly associated with colour pattern evolution in butterflies.
source: One of these genes, cortex, has been repeatedly associated with colour pattern evolution in butterflies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: cortex is a major determinant of scale cell identity in multiple Heliconius species.
source: Here we carried out CRISPR knockouts in multiple Heliconius species and show that cortex is a major determinant of scale cell identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR knockout experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Chromatin accessibility profiling and introgression scans identified cis-regulatory regions associated with discrete phenotypic switches.
source: Chromatin accessibility profiling and introgression scans identified cis-regulatory regions associated with discrete phenotypic switches.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ATAC-seq and Twisst analysis data in the manuscript.

claim: CRISPR perturbation of cis-regulatory regions in black hindwing genotypes recreated a yellow bar.
source: CRISPR perturbation of these regions in black hindwing genotypes recreated a yellow bar, revealing their spatially limited activity.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR experiments targeting CREs described in the Results section.

claim: In the H. melpomene/timareta lineage, the candidate CRE from yellow-barred phenotype morphs is interrupted by a transposable element.
source: In the H. melpomene/timareta lineage, the candidate CRE from yellow-barred phenotype morphs is interrupted by a transposable element, suggesting that cis-regulatory structural variation underlies these mimetic adaptations.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data and coverage analysis showing TE insertions in yellow-barred morphs.

claim: cortex functionally controls scale colour fate.
source: Our work shows that cortex functionally controls scale colour fate and that its cis-regulatory regions control a phenotypic switch in a modular and pattern-specific fashion.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout experiments showing transformation of scale types.

claim: cortex cis-regulatory regions control a phenotypic switch in a modular and pattern-specific fashion.
source: Our work shows that cortex functionally controls scale colour fate and that its cis-regulatory regions control a phenotypic switch in a modular and pattern-specific fashion.
evidence: This is supported by CRE knockout experiments that produce spatially restricted yellow bar phenotypes.

claim: The genetic locus containing cortex was originally identified in the genus Heliconius as controlling differences in yellow and white wing patterns in H. melpomene and H. erato.
source: The genetic locus containing cortex was originally identified in the genus Heliconius as controlling differences in yellow and white wing patterns in H. melpomene and H. erato (Figure 1a) and the polymorphism in yellow, white, black, and orange elements in H. numata. This was inferred using a combination of association mapping and gene expression data (Joron et al., 2006; Nadeau et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous mapping studies.

claim: The cortex locus has been repeatedly implicated in controlling colour pattern variation among divergent Lepidoptera.
source: The same locus has also been repeatedly implicated in controlling colour pattern variation among divergent Lepidoptera, including the peppered moth Biston betularia and other geometrids, the silkmoth Bombyx mori, and other butterflies such as Junonia coenia, Bicyclus anynana, and Papilio clytia (Beldade et al., 2009; van der Burg et al., 2020; Ito et al., 2016; VanKuren et al., 2019; Van't Hof et al., 2019; Van't Hof et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in different lepidopteran species.

claim: Cortex is an insect-specific gene showing closest homology to the cdc20/fizzy family of cell cycle regulators.
source: Cortex, on the other hand, is an insect-specific gene showing closest homology to the cdc20/fizzy family of cell cycle regulators (Chu et al., 2001; Nadeau et al., 2016; Pesin and Orr-Weaver, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: The lepidopteran orthologue of cortex displays rapid sequence evolution.
source: The lepidopteran orthologue of cortex displays rapid sequence evolution and has acquired novel expression domains that correlate with melanic wing patterns in Heliconius (Nadeau et al., 2016; Saenko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing long branch lengths and citations to previous studies.

claim: cortex has acquired novel expression domains that correlate with melanic wing patterns in Heliconius.
source: The lepidopteran orthologue of cortex displays rapid sequence evolution and has acquired novel expression domains that correlate with melanic wing patterns in Heliconius (Nadeau et al., 2016; Saenko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous expression studies.

claim: Most of the pattern variation in Heliconius is created by differences in the distribution of just three major scale cell types: Type I (yellow/white), Type II (black), and Type III (red/orange/brown).
source: While fantastically diverse, most of the pattern variation in Heliconius is created by differences in the distribution of just three major scale cell types: Type I (yellow/white), Type II (black), and Type III (red/orange/brown) (Aymone et al., 2013; Gilbert et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on scale cell types.

claim: Type I yellow scales contain the ommochrome precursor 3-hydroxykynurenine (3-OHK).
source: Type I yellow scales contain the ommochrome precursor 3-hydroxykynurenine (3-OHK) (Finkbeiner et al., 2017; Koch, 1993; Reed et al., 2008), whereas Type I white scales lack pigment, and the white colour is the result of the scale cell ultrastructure (i.e. structural white) (Gilbert et al., 1987) (see Figure 9f).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: Type I white scales lack pigment, and the white colour is the result of the scale cell ultrastructure.
source: Type I yellow scales contain the ommochrome precursor 3-hydroxykynurenine (3-OHK) (Finkbeiner et al., 2017; Koch, 1993; Reed et al., 2008), whereas Type I white scales lack pigment, and the white colour is the result of the scale cell ultrastructure (i.e. structural white) (Gilbert et al., 1987) (see Figure 9f).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and SEM data in Figure 9.

claim: Type I scales are characterised by the presence of a lamina covering the scale windows and by microribs joining the larger longitudinal ridges.
source: Structurally, Type I scales are characterised by the presence of a lamina covering the scale windows and by microribs joining the larger longitudinal ridges.
evidence: This is supported by SEM data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Type II scale cells are pigmented with melanin, have larger crossribs and lack a lamina covering the scale windows.
source: In contrast, Type II scale cells are pigmented with melanin, have larger crossribs and lack a lamina covering the scale windows.
evidence: This is supported by SEM data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Type III scale cells contain the red ommochrome pigments xanthommatin and dihydroxanthommatin.
source: Finally, Type III scale cells contain the red ommochrome pigments xanthommatin and dihydroxanthommatin and are characterised by larger spacing between crossribs and ridges.
evidence: This is supported by previous biochemical studies and SEM data.

claim: cortex is differentially expressed between colour pattern morphs in fifth-instar larvae in both H. erato and H. melpomene.
source: In fifth-instar larvae, cortex is differentially expressed in both species between the two colour pattern morphs, with cortex showing the highest adjusted p-value (Benjamini and Hochberg correction) for any gene in the genome at this stage in H. erato (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: cortex transcripts were differentially expressed in opposite directions in H. melpomene and H. erato.
source: Interestingly, cortex transcripts were differentially expressed in opposite directions in the two species, with higher expression in the melanic hindwing morph in H. melpomene and in the yellow banded morph in H. erato.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data.

claim: dome/wash is differentially expressed at Day 1 pupae between morphs in both H. melpomene and H. erato.
source: This pattern is reversed for dome/wash in Day 1 pupae, where a statistically higher proportion of transcripts are detected in H. melpomene rosina (yellow) and in H. erato hydara (melanic) (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2 supplements.

claim: cortex is an insect-specific member of the cdc20 family with no clear cortex homologs found outside of the Neoptera.
source: Our analysis finds strong monophyletic support for cortex as an insect-specific member of the cdc20 family, with no clear cortex homologs found outside of the Neoptera (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: cortex is evolving rapidly within the Neoptera lineage.
source: Branch lengths indicate cortex is evolving rapidly within the lineage, despite displaying conserved anaphase promoting complex (APC/C binding motifs, including the C-Box and IR tail Figure 2—figure supplement 6; Chu et al., 2001; Pesin and Orr-Weaver, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing long branch lengths.

claim: Cortex transcripts at fifth-instar localised distally in forewings and hindwings of both H. erato and H. melpomene species.
source: Cortex transcripts at this stage localised distally in forewings and hindwings of both species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In H. erato demophoon hindwings, cortex expression was strongest at the intervein midline but extends across vein compartments.
source: In H. erato demophoon hindwings, expression was strongest at the intervein midline, but extends across vein compartments covering the distal portion of both forewing and hindwing (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In H. erato hydara hindwings, cortex transcripts are more strongly localised to the intervein midline forming a sharper intervein expression domain.
source: By contrast, in H. erato hydara hindwings, cortex transcripts are more strongly localised to the intervein midline forming a sharper intervein expression domain (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Targeting of the cortex gene in H. erato morphs produced patches of ectopic yellow and white scales spanning regions across both forewings and hindwings.
source: Targeting of the cortex gene in H. erato morphs produced patches of ectopic yellow and white scales spanning regions across both forewings and hindwings (Figure 4—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutant clones from cortex knockouts were not restricted to any specific wing region, affecting scales in both proximal and distal portions of wings.
source: Mutant clones were not restricted to any specific wing region, affecting scales in both proximal and distal portions of wings.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout phenotypes shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The same effect on scale pigmentation from cortex knockout was also observed in H. melpomene morphs.
source: The same effect on scale pigmentation was also observed in H. melpomene morphs, with mutant clones affecting both distal and proximal regions in forewings and hindwings (Figure 5a–c).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: cortex knockout in H. erato hydara caused transformation of red scales to white scales and some showing an intermediate phenotype.
source: Clones affecting this region caused what appears to be an asymmetric deposition of pigment across the scales, as well as transformation to white, unpigmented scales (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout phenotypes shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: A positional effect was observed in cortex knockouts where ectopic scales in the forewing and anterior compartment of the hindwing shifted to yellow, and posterior hindwing scales became white.
source: Furthermore, we observed a positional effect, where ectopic scales in the forewing and anterior compartment of the hindwing shifted to yellow, and posterior hindwing scales became white (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 5d).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout phenotypes shown in Figure 4.

claim: cortex has a conserved function in switching scale cell fates across the Heliconius radiation and in nymphalids.
source: To further test the conservation of cortex function across the Heliconius radiation, as well as nymphalids as a whole, we knocked out cortex in H. charithonia and H. hecale melicerta, outgroups to H. erato and H. melpomene, respectively, and Danaus plexippus as an outgroup to all Heliconiini. Again, ectopic yellow and white scales appeared throughout the wing surface in all species, suggesting a conserved function with respect to scale development among butterflies (Figure 5d–f, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–5).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout experiments in multiple species shown in Figure 5.

claim: cortex is likely developmentally lethal based on high mortality rates in CRISPR experiments.
source: The high rate of mosaicism combined with high mortality rates suggests cortex is likely developmentally lethal.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed mortality rates in CRISPR experiments.

claim: Cortex protein is localized in the nucleus across the epithelium of H. erato demophoon pupal hindwings without restriction to specific pattern elements.
source: To test this hypothesis, we developed a Cortex polyclonal antibody and found nuclear expression across the epithelium of H. erato demophoon pupal hindwings without restriction to specific pattern elements (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Cortex protein was detected in fifth-instar larvae in a similar pattern to mRNA, with expression visible at the intervein midline of developing wings.
source: In fifth-instar larvae, Cortex protein was detected in a similar pattern to mRNA, with expression visible at the intervein midline of developing wings (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Cortex was detected across the entire wing surface from 24 hr after pupal formation (a.p.f), until 80 hr a.p.f.
source: Cortex was then detected across the entire wing surface from 24 hr after pupal formation (a.p.f), until 80 hr a.p.f in our time series (Figure 6b–d, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Cortex localization remained nuclear throughout pupal wing development and appears equal in intensity across hindwing colour pattern elements.
source: Localisation remained nuclear throughout development and appears equal in intensity across hindwing colour pattern elements (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: ATAC-seq identified many accessible chromatin peaks surrounding cortex.
source: We observed many accessible chromatin 'peaks' surrounding cortex (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), each of which could represent a potentially active CRE.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Twisst analysis identified a strong signal of association ~8 kb downstream of the annotated cortex stop codon that overlapped with a clear ATAC-seq peak.
source: This method identified a strong signal of association ~8 kb downstream of the annotated cortex stop codon, that overlapped with a clear ATAC-seq peak (Figure 7a,b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Twisst analysis and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Knockout of the CRE ~8 kb downstream of cortex in H. melpomene melpomene resulted in the appearance of yellow scales in a yellow bar-like pattern.
source: Indeed, upon KO of this CRE we recovered mKOs consistent with a modular enhancer driving cortex expression in a yellow bar-specific pattern, with no clones exhibiting yellow scales extending out of the region that forms the yellow bar (Figure 7c, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR CRE knockout experiments shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Targeting of a different CRE ~10 kb 3' of the H. melpomene conserved CRE in H. erato hydara resulted in a yellow bar phenotype.
source: Remarkably, targeting of this CRE resulted in a yellow bar phenotype in the melanic H. erato hydara, with no clones containing yellow scales extending beyond the region that forms the yellow bar (Figure 7c, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR CRE knockout experiments shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The CREs interact with the cortex promoter as shown by Hi-C data.
source: For both CREs, we found a statistically significant interaction between CRE and promoter, indicating the observed effect is likely due to the CRE interacting with the cortex promoter, and not a different gene at the locus (Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: A characteristic drop in coverage was observed at the targeted CRE in all H. melpomene and H. timareta morphs exhibiting a yellow bar phenotype.
source: We observed a characteristic drop in coverage at the targeted CRE in all H. melpomene and H. timareta morphs exhibiting a yellow bar phenotype, while no drop was detected in morphs with a melanic hindwing (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing coverage analysis shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Two transposable element insertions were found in H. melpomene rosina spanning the CRE peak.
source: Surprisingly, we found two transposable element (TE) insertions in H. melpomene rosina with a Helitron-like TE found spanning the CRE peak, suggesting that the coverage drop is instead due to an insertion of repetitive sequence, rather than a deletion.
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The same TE signatures were found in three other yellow-barred morphs (H. melpomene bellula, H. melpomene amaryllis, and H. timareta tristero).
source: We next assayed three other yellow-barred morphs (H. melpomene bellula, H. melpomene amaryllis, and H. timareta tristero) and found the same TE signatures in all three populations (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), suggesting the TE insertions are likely shared through introgression.
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: No similar signature of reduced coverage was observed in co-mimetic morphs of H. erato.
source: No similar signature of reduced coverage was observed in co-mimetic morphs of H. erato, suggesting that sequence divergence is responsible for the evolution of the yellow bar CRE in this species (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing coverage analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cortex mutant scales show ultrastructural shifts consistent with partial homeosis.
source: We observed ultrastructural shifts that are consistent with partial homeosis in cortex mutant scales in both H. melpomene and H. erato (Figure 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by SEM data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Wild-type blue and black scales have crossribs at a spacing of ~0.6 µm, lack lamina between ridges and crossribs, and have no prominent microribs.
source: Wild-type blue and black scales have crossribs at a spacing of ~0.6 µm, lack lamina between ridges and crossribs, and have no prominent microribs, while both wild-type and mutant Type I scales have no prominent crossribs, lamina that fills the spaces between the microribs and ridges, and prominent microribs at a spacing of ~0.2 µm (Figure 9a–d, Figure 9—source data 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by SEM measurements shown in Figure 9.

claim: Both wild-type and mutant Type I scales have no prominent crossribs, lamina that fills the spaces between the microribs and ridges, and prominent microribs at a spacing of ~0.2 µm.
source: Wild-type blue and black scales have crossribs at a spacing of ~0.6 µm, lack lamina between ridges and crossribs, and have no prominent microribs, while both wild-type and mutant Type I scales have no prominent crossribs, lamina that fills the spaces between the microribs and ridges, and prominent microribs at a spacing of ~0.2 µm (Figure 9a–d, Figure 9—source data 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by SEM measurements shown in Figure 9.

claim: A consistent difference between all Type I scales (mutant and wild type) is the presence of a lamina covering the inter-ridge space.
source: A consistent difference between all Type I scales (mutant and wild type) is the presence of a lamina covering the inter-ridge space (Figure 9f).
evidence: This is supported by SEM data shown in Figure 9f.

claim: Red scales (Type III) within a cortex coding KO clone take on an aberrant structure and pigmentation.
source: Red scales (Type III) that are within a coding KO clone take on an aberrant structure and pigmentation. Scales were frequently found to be curled up laterally, and while ommochrome pigment is sometimes visibly deposited in the scale, it is granular in appearance rather than diffuse throughout the scale (Figure 9e, Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by SEM data shown in Figure 9e.

claim: cortex is a causative gene that specifies melanic and red (Type II and Type III) scale cell identity in Heliconius.
source: Here, we demonstrate that cortex is a causative gene that specifies melanic and red (Type II and Type III) scale cell identity in Heliconius and acts by influencing both downstream pigmentation pathways and scale cell ultrastructure.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout experiments showing transformation of scale types.

claim: cortex acts by influencing both downstream pigmentation pathways and scale cell ultrastructure.
source: Here, we demonstrate that cortex is a causative gene that specifies melanic and red (Type II and Type III) scale cell identity in Heliconius and acts by influencing both downstream pigmentation pathways and scale cell ultrastructure.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout experiments showing changes in both pigmentation and scale ultrastructure.

claim: cortex is under the control of modular enhancers that control the switch between mimetic yellow bar phenotypes in both H. melpomene and H. erato.
source: We also show that cortex is under the control of modular enhancers that appear to control the switch between mimetic yellow bar phenotypes in both H. melpomene and H. erato.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR CRE knockout experiments showing spatially restricted phenotypes.

claim: cortex acts as a key scale cell specification switch across the wing surface of Heliconius butterflies.
source: Our combination of expression studies and functional knockouts demonstrate that this gene acts as a key scale cell specification switch across the wing surface of Heliconius butterflies, and thus has the potential to generate much broader pattern variation than previously described patterning genes.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout experiments showing effects across the entire wing surface.

claim: Cortex protein localises to the nucleus in Heliconius pupal wings.
source: Immunostainings show that Cortex protein localises to the nucleus in Heliconius pupal wings, suggesting a possible interaction with the APC/C in butterfly scale building cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ploidy levels in Lepidoptera scale cells have been shown to correlate with pigmentation state, where increased ploidy and scale size lead to darker scales.
source: Ploidy levels in Lepidoptera scale cells have been shown to correlate with pigmentation state, where increased ploidy and scale size lead to darker scales (Cho and Nijhout, 2013; Iwata and Otaki, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: cortex may be modulating ploidy levels by inducing endoreplication cycles in developing scale cells.
source: cortex may thus be modulating ploidy levels by inducing endoreplication cycles in developing scale cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on known functions of cortex homologs in Drosophila.

claim: In H. melpomene, a clear peak of association with the presence of accessible chromatin marks was narrowed down ~8 kb downstream of the annotated cortex stop codon.
source: In H.melpomene, we were able to narrow down a clear peak of association with the presence of accessible chromatin marks and showed that KO of this region results in the appearance of a yellow bar phenotype in black hindwing morphs (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq and Twisst analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: When targeting the homologous peak in H. erato, no phenotype was recovered.
source: Interestingly, when targeting the homologous peak in H. erato, we failed to recover any type of phenotype, but were able to induce the appearance of a yellow bar through the targeting of an adjacent peak, not present in the H. melpomene datasets, indicating that an independently evolved CRE is driving this phenotype in H. erato.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR CRE knockout experiments.

claim: An independently evolved CRE is driving the yellow bar phenotype in H. erato.
source: Interestingly, when targeting the homologous peak in H. erato, we failed to recover any type of phenotype, but were able to induce the appearance of a yellow bar through the targeting of an adjacent peak, not present in the H. melpomene datasets, indicating that an independently evolved CRE is driving this phenotype in H. erato.
evidence: This is inferred from the different CRE locations in the two species.

claim: The CREs are enhancers that are able to drive cortex expression in a yellow bar specific manner.
source: These results, coupled with the coding KOs, suggests that the CREs are enhancers that are able to drive cortex expression in a yellow bar specific manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatially restricted phenotypes of CRE knockouts.

claim: A large 690 bp TE insertion 5' of the peak of interest and a Helitron-like sequence overlapping the peak were found in H. melpomene rosina.
source: Upon further investigation, we found a large 690 bp TE insertion 5' of the peak of interest as well as a Helitron-like sequence overlapping the peak in H. melpomene rosina.
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: Recurrent TE insertions across the CRE region are driving the evolution of the yellow bar phenotype in H. melpomene populations.
source: This raises the interesting possibility that this portion of the enhancer might contain the binding sites necessary to drive cortex in a yellow bar specific manner, and that recurrent TE insertions across this region are driving the evolution of this phenotype in H. melpomene populations.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed TE insertions.

claim: The TE insertion is observed in mimetic morphs of H. timareta, suggesting adaptive introgression of this region.
source: We also note that this insertion is observed in mimetic morphs of a different species, H. timareta, with which H. melpomene has previously been described to share regulatory regions at other patterning loci via adaptive introgression (Morris et al., 2019; Wallbank et al., 2016). Thus, adaptive introgression of this region and its structural variants is likely facilitating mimicry in this system (Heliconius Genome Consortium et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the shared TE signatures and previous evidence of introgression at other loci.

claim: cortex and WntA are master regulators of scale cell identity.
source: This work underscores the importance of two patterning loci, cortex and WntA, as master regulators of scale cell identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the broad effects of knockouts of both genes.

claim: Both cortex and WntA are upregulated early in wing development and have broad effects on pattern variation.
source: Both are upregulated early in wing development and have broad effects on pattern variation (Concha et al., 2019; Nadeau et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by expression data and citations to previous studies.

claim: WntA modulates forewing band shape in Heliconius by delineating boundaries around patterns elements.
source: The signalling molecule WntA modulates forewing band shape in Heliconius by delineating boundaries around patterns elements, and is expressed in close association with future pattern elements (Concha et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: WntA KOs shift scale cell identity to all three cell types (I, II, and III), depending on genetic background.
source: Unlike cortex mutants, WntA KOs shift scale cell identity to all three cell types (I, II, and III), depending on genetic background.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous WntA knockout studies.

claim: WntA acts as a spatial patterning signal inducing or inhibiting colour in specific wing elements, in contrast to cortex, which acts as an 'on-off' switch across all scales on the butterfly wing.
source: Thus, WntA acts as a spatial patterning signal inducing or inhibiting colour in specific wing elements, in contrast to cortex, which acts as an 'on-off' switch across all scales on the butterfly wing.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the phenotypes of WntA and cortex knockouts.

claim: cortex knockouts lead to shifts in scale fate irrespective of WntA expression.
source: Interestingly, cortex knockouts lead to shifts in scale fate irrespective of WntA expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cortex knockouts affect all wing regions.

claim: cortex is required as an inductive signal to allow WntA to signal further melanisation, or two independent ways to melanise a scale are available to the developing wing.
source: This suggests either that cortex is required as an inductive signal to allow WntA to signal further melanisation, or that two, independent ways to melanise a scale are available to the developing wing.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: Under certain conditions cortex is sufficient to induce the development of black scales, but WntA is also required as a further signal for melanisation in some genetic backgrounds.
source: This indicates that while under certain conditions cortex is sufficient to induce the development of black scales, WntA is also required as a further signal for melanisation in some genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This is inferred from WntA knockout phenotypes in different genetic backgrounds.

claim: Genetic evidence for epistasis between cortex and WntA loci is seen in crossing experiments.
source: This is also consistent with genetic evidence for epistasis between these two loci seen in crossing experiments, whereby the yellow bar in H. erato favorinus results from an interaction between the Cortex and WntA loci (Mallet, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous crossing experiments.

claim: cortex is one of the earliest regulators and sets scale differentiation to a specific pathway switching between Type I (yellow/white) and Type II/III (black/red) scales.
source: Under a simple model (Figure 10), cortex is one of the earliest regulators and sets scale differentiation to a specific pathway switches between Type I (yellow/white) and Type II/III (black/red) scales.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observed phenotypes and expression patterns.

claim: A differentiating presumptive scale cell (PSC) receiving a Cortex input becomes Type II/III competent, with complete Type III differentiation occurring in the presence of optix expression.
source: Thus, we can envision a differentiating presumptive scale cell (PSC) receiving a Cortex input as becoming Type II/III competent, with complete Type III differentiation occurring in the presence of optix expression (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observed phenotypes and previous optix studies.

claim: cortex expression is required for either downstream signalling to optix or to induce a permissive scale morphology for the synthesis and deposition of red pigment in future scales.
source: Therefore, cortex expression is required for either downstream signalling to optix or to induce a permissive scale morphology for the synthesis and deposition of red pigment in future scales.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed phenotypes of cortex knockouts affecting red scales.

claim: Cortex is necessary for the induction of Type III scale cells but insufficient for their proper development.
source: Cortex is thus necessary for the induction of Type III scale cells but insufficient for their proper development.
evidence: This is inferred from the aberrant red scale phenotypes in cortex knockouts.

claim: A PSC lacking a Cortex input differentiates into a Type I scale, whose pigmentation state depends on the presence of the transcription factor aristaless1 (al1).
source: Conversely, a PSC lacking a Cortex input differentiates into a Type I scale, whose pigmentation state depends on the presence of the transcription factor aristaless1 (al1), where al1 is responsible for inducing a switch from yellow to white scales in Heliconius by affecting the deposition of the yellow pigment 3-OHK (Westerman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observed phenotypes and previous al1 studies.

claim: The uptake of 3-OHK from the haemolymph occurs very late in wing development, right before the adult ecloses.
source: The uptake of 3-OHK from the haemolymph occurs very late in wing development, right before the adult ecloses (Reed et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: cortex mKOs revealed a shift to both yellow and white scales, with their appearance being positionally dependent.
source: Our cortex mKOs revealed a shift to both yellow and white scales, with their appearance being positionally dependent; more distally located scales generally switch to white, while more proximal scales become yellow.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR knockout phenotypes.

claim: The pigmentation state of cortex mutant scales is likely controlled by differences in al1 expression varying between wing sections in different ways across morphs.
source: This pigmentation state is likely controlled by differences in al1 expression varying between wing sections in different ways across morphs.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed positional effects.

claim: The switch induced by Cortex is likely not a simple binary toggle, and is perhaps dependent on a given protein threshold or heterochrony in expression rather than presence/absence.
source: However, the switch induced by Cortex under this model is likely not a simple binary toggle, and is perhaps dependent on a given protein threshold or heterochrony in expression rather than presence/absence, as we find that Cortex protein also localises to the presumptive yellow bar in developing pupal wings.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation that Cortex protein is present across the entire wing.

claim: Other linked genes such as dome/wash may also be playing a role in controlling pattern switches between Heliconius morphs.
source: Moreover, the RNA-seq data presented suggests other linked genes may also be playing a role in controlling pattern switches between Heliconius morphs. In particular, we report the presence of a bi-cistronic transcript containing the ORFs of the genes dome/wash, which are differentially expressed during early pupal wing development.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential expression of dome/wash.

claim: dome/wash are differentially expressed during early pupal wing development.
source: In particular, we report the presence of a bi-cistronic transcript containing the ORFs of the genes dome/wash, which are differentially expressed during early pupal wing development.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Multiple linked genes may co-operate during Heliconius wing development to drive pattern diversity.
source: It raises the possibility that multiple linked genes co-operate during Heliconius wing development to drive pattern diversity.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the differential expression of multiple genes at the locus.

claim: In the locally polymorphic H. numata, all wing pattern variation is controlled by inversions surrounding cortex and dome/wash, both of which are also differentially expressed in H. numata.
source: It is noteworthy that in the locally polymorphic H. numata, all wing pattern variation is controlled by inversions surrounding cortex and dome/wash, both of which are also differentially expressed in H. numata (Saenko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies on H. numata.

claim: Evolution has favoured the interaction of multiple genes at the cortex locus that have since become locked into a supergene in H. numata.
source: This raises the interesting possibility that evolution has favoured the interaction of multiple genes at the locus that have since become locked into a supergene in H. numata.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation of multiple differentially expressed genes at the locus.

claim: A conserved feature of the cortex locus in Lepidoptera is the presence of large intergenic regions surrounding the gene.
source: A conserved feature of the cortex locus in Lepidoptera is the presence of large intergenic regions surrounding the gene, with evidence these may be acting as modular cis-regulatory switches in Heliconius (Enciso-Romero et al., 2017; Van Belleghem et al., 2017), fitting the predicted structure of input-output genes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: cortex expression appears not to be restricted to any particular colour pattern element in any given species/morph, and yet is capable of producing a switch-like output (Type I vs Type II/III scales).
source: Unlike canonical input-output loci however, cortex expression appears not to be restricted to any particular colour pattern element in any given species/morph, and yet is capable of producing a switch-like output (Type I vs Type II/III scales).
evidence: This is supported by expression and knockout data.

claim: Two independent CREs in H. melpomene and H. erato evolved to control the presence/absence of a yellow hindwing bar.
source: Furthermore, our work shows that two independent CREs in H. melpomene and H. erato evolved to control the presence/absence of a yellow hindwing bar.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR CRE knockout experiments showing spatially restricted phenotypes.

claim: dome appears to have duplicated in the ancestor of H. erato and H. melpomene, resulting in a full-length copy and a further copy exhibiting truncations at the C-terminus (domeless-truncated).
source: In Heliconius, dome appears to have duplicated in the ancestor of H. erato and H. melpomene, resulting in a full-length copy (referred to here as domeless) and a further copy exhibiting truncations at the C-terminus (domeless-truncated [dome-trunc]) (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: dome and wash are transcribed as a single bi-cistronic gene.
source: Transcriptomic and previous evidence (Lewis et al., 2020) also indicates that dome and wash are transcribed as a single bi-cistronic gene (Figure 1—figure supplements 3–4).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Overall KO efficiency was low when compared to similar studies in Heliconius, with observed wing phenotype to hatched eggs ratios ranging from 0.3% to 4.8%.
source: Overall KO efficiency was low when compared to similar studies in Heliconius (Concha et al., 2019; Mazo-Vargas et al., 2017), with observed wing phenotype to hatched eggs ratios ranging from 0.3% to 4.8%.
evidence: This is supported by data on CRISPR injection outcomes.

claim: Lethality was high in cortex CRISPR experiments, with hatched to adult ratios ranging from 8.1% to 29.8%.
source: Lethality was also high, with hatched to adult ratios ranging from 8.1% to 29.8% (Figure 4—source data 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by data on CRISPR injection outcomes.

claim: TBLASTN searches against arthropod genome and transcriptome NCBI repositories did not recover Cortex homologues outside of the Neoptera lineage.
source: TBLASTN searches against arthropod genome and transcriptome NCBI repositories did not recover Cortex homologues outside of the Neoptera lineage.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: In H. melpomene dome-trunc maintains only the N-terminal half of the gene, suggesting dome-trunc is undergoing pseudogenisation.
source: Protein alignments indicate that in both H. erato and H. melpomene, dome-trunc maintains only the N-terminal half of the gene, suggesting dome-trunc is undergoing pseudogenisation.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supported by protein alignment data.

claim: Peaks indicating cis-regulatory activity were observed upstream of dome for all samples, whereas no peaks were present upstream of the start of wash, indicating a shared promoter for dome/wash.
source: Peaks, indicating cis-regulatory activity, were observed upstream of dome for all samples, whereas no peaks were present upstream of the start of wash, indicating a shared promoter for dome/wash.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and supported by ATAC-seq data.
